en: The metal loading ramp of a Philippine jeepney acts as an inclined plane, making it easier to push heavy cargo upward.
Wearing rubber tsinelas on wet tiled floors is dangerous because water reduces the friction between the rubber and the tiles.
When a ripe carabao mango falls from a tree in Guimaras, Earth's gravity pulls the fruit straight down to the ground.
The black sand beaches of Ilocos Norte contain magnetite, a magnetic mineral that can be attracted to a standard bar magnet.
The Agus Hydroelectric Power Plants in Lanao del Norte generate electricity by using the kinetic energy of flowing water to spin turbines.
Thousands of aninipot fireflies along Bohol’s Loboc River produce their own light energy through a chemical reaction inside their abdomens.
During a tinikling dance, the clapper produces sound energy by striking the bamboo poles together, causing the air around them to vibrate.
The MakBan geothermal power plant in Laguna generates electricity by harnessing the natural heat energy from the magma beneath Mount Makiling.
A dropped pabitin basket transforms from stored potential energy into kinetic energy as it falls toward the eager children below.
Sugarcane plantations in Negros Occidental store chemical energy in their sweet juices, which factories convert into useful bioethanol fuel.
A taho vendor uses a wooden carrying pole as a first-class lever, balancing the heavy buckets of tofu and syrup on their shoulders.
A wooden kariton cart with round wheels rolls easily across the market floor because rolling friction is much weaker than sliding friction.
